# Introduction {#intro}

```{r fig.align='center', echo=FALSE, out.width='100%', fig.cap='IOBRpy workflow'}
knitr::include_graphics('assets/img/IOBRpy.png', dpi = NA)
```

This tutorial presents a reproducible IOBRpy workflow that starts with public paired-end FASTQ files. The main `runall` command uses STAR and produces quality-control files, alignments, a TPM matrix, signature scores, six default TME analyses, ligand-receptor scores, and TRUST4 results. Separate chapters cover BayesPrism, TME clustering, and HLA typing.

## What you will produce

The complete workflow creates:

```text
results/gbm-demo/
├── 01-qc/
├── 02-star/
├── 03-tpm/
├── 04-signatures/
├── 05-tme/
├── 06-LR_cal/
├── 07-TCRBCR/
├── 08-bayesprism/
├── 09-tme-cluster/
└── 10-hla/
```

By the end of the tutorial, you will be able to:

- obtain complete paired-end FASTQ files from a public repository;
- build a STAR genome index that matches the annotation;
- inspect inputs and validate workflow parameters with `map` and `recommend`;
- run FASTQ-to-TPM, TME, ligand-receptor, and TRUST4 analysis with `runall`;
- run BayesPrism and TME clustering from the matrices created by `runall`;
- run HLA typing from the STAR BAM files;
- replace the teaching data with your own FASTQ files.

## Teaching dataset

The example uses four pretreatment glioblastoma samples from [PRJNA482620](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/bioproject/PRJNA482620). The source study is [Zhao et al., Nature Medicine (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-019-0349-y).

| Run | Patient | Teaching group | Time point | Library |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| SRR8281218 | P20 | NR | Pre | paired-end RNA-seq |
| SRR8281226 | P53 | NR | Pre | paired-end RNA-seq |
| SRR8281245 | P100 | R | Pre | paired-end RNA-seq |
| SRR8281243 | P101 | R | Pre | paired-end RNA-seq |

> **Teaching limitation:** Four samples are suitable for learning file organization, command execution, and output structure. This cohort is too small for stable group-level inference.

## Why the main workflow uses STAR

IOBRpy `runall` supports both Salmon and STAR. This book uses STAR because the HLA chapter requires aligned BAM files. Salmon quantifies transcripts but does not produce the BAM input required by `hla_typing`.

STAR requires more memory, storage, and run time than Salmon. The complete FASTQ files and human genome index require substantial disk space.

## Conventions

- Commands are written for Bash on Linux, macOS, or WSL2.
- Expression matrices use **genes × samples** orientation.
- All analysis commands use the native `iobrpy` interface.
- Paths are relative to the `IOBRpy_book/` repository root.
